episode.episode: Philips Hue: The smart home’s light bulb moment
episode.showDescription: Version History is a show about the best gadgets ever. And the worst ones. And the ones that might have changed the world, if they ever actually shipped. Every week, your favorite people from The Verge and beyond hang out to tell and debate the story of a gadget, app, website, or any other tech product, and try to determine the item’s true legacy. Because not every product is a hit, but every product has a story. And the ones that really matter aren’t always the ones you think. From the Verge and the Vox Media Podcast Network.
episode.episodeDescription: The humble light bulb might be the ultimate success story in the smart home. Our connected, adaptable homes are supposed to be customizable, connected to everything, and incredibly easy to use, and nothing has made that work quite like Philips Hue lights. In this episode, The Verge's David Pierce and Jennifer Pattison Tuohy are joined by smart home journalist and expert Richard Gunther to tell the Hue's story. We trace the product's history from its origins in the smartphone revolution, try to figure out how Philips managed to turn a staggeringly expensive lightbulb into a must-have gadget, and look at whether there's even more invention left in the future of lighting. We’re also on video! Check us out on YouTube. Subscribe to The Verge for unlimited access to theverge.com, subscriber-exclusive newsletters, and our ad-free podcast feed. We love hearing from you! transcript_window.text: We don't have time to go into all of the strange things that Philips has been involved with over the years.
But like, I think of Philips as like the company that makes my razor much, much more than that.
But anyway, so inside of Philips, there are basically two things happening sort of simultaneously on the lighting team.
Again, the iPhone has come out.
And so there's a team that starts to work on just building apps.
They think it might be cool to control some of the things they're already starting to make.
They made this product called the Living Colors Lamp.
I have a clip of this lamp just for anybody who doesn't remember.
It's like shockingly early little bit of color changing lamp.
Let me just play this for you.
Sometimes a room can seem, well, boring.
But the right LED light can change all that in the flash.
And bring your space.
Look at TV.
A Philips Living Colors Iris is the perfect way to...
just gives you the sense of the time we're talking about.
High -power LEDs deliver 16 million colors to choose from.
And with the easy -to -use remote control, you can adjust brightness to set the mode you want.
It's timeless and distinctive.
So this gives you a sense, right?
This is very much a smart lamp, but it is a sort of hacky pre -smartphone digital one.
But you can change the color of your light.
And this is already a meaningful, exciting new thing.

And so there's a team at Philips that is like, OK, wouldn't it be cool if you could change the colors on your light with this touchscreen that people are starting to have in their pockets called the iPhone?
And then there's this other team working on the living color stuff led by this guy named George Yanni, who, Jen, you just spoke to the other day.
In fact, George, who is the co -founder of Hue, is a theoretical physicist.
